For those who witnessed Digg go down, how does the current drama compare?

Digg instituted a number of changes to give preference to paid submissions while simultaneously removing the Digg users ability to downvote. When the community complained Digg simply ignored it and doubled down on the changes.

I find it similar to Reddit in that it seems Reddit is trying to make a safer environment for advertisers, but I don't personally remember Digg censoring their site as much as Reddit is doing now. The community is reacting very similarly to the Digg community from 5 years ago.

I find Reddit's censorship much more troubling personally than Digg's bone headed business decisions.

Will it always be inevitable for the largest mainstream sites to sell out? I know there are giant sites like Wikipedia that stay alive through donations, or multi-faceted corporate groups like Google+ being subsidised by Google.com-search (IE there aren't adds on G+, though in the future there may be, or paid posts etc., but pretty much G+ can lose the company billions a year, and it will survive anyway because it's in their web) - but a website as popular as reddit, with a young/ad-blocking audience that may not donate as much or be worth as much to advertisers - it must cost a lot to host and develop/ maintain/ secure a website like that - and so the owners and investors must always be pushing to up revenue in some ways...

Not that I'm saying it's ok or a valid excuse.. but it'll probably happen to any top website.. ?

It should be noted that when Digg went down, reddit had been around for some time and the quality of discussion was not too different from what we have here, at the time. When the Digg community went over, there was a noticeable drop in the quality of posts and comments overnight to the extent that it was shocking. Reddit never recovered.

Meanwhile, the influx of reddit users hasn't actually destroyed the content quality on voat, at least not nearly to the same extent. In fact, while there is/was an initial dip, the newest wave of users seem to be very receptive to this notion that a large part of the existing voat community takes the content quality very seriously, and are stepping up to the plate. I praise and thank new users for this every chance I get.

I actually preferred dig to redirect before they made the changes, but it was almost overnight that it seemed to change. The quantity of new content was the first thing I noticed that changed, then the quality. I used both sites for awhile, but at one point reddit was much more interesting and I never went back. This time I left because reddit.com quality has dropped, but mainly because it wasn't fun anymore. Anything you said was lost in the crowd. With voat I don't feel like I have to be an asset to get some karma

I was an avid digg user but I all I remember about the downfall was how they tried to make it like twitter, where you had to follow people to get content. I didn't want that at all. Plus there was weekly drama about front page auctions etc.

The early days of reddit wasn't very inspiring, either. The whole front page was lifehacker links to top-ten lists of whatever, and political battles between news links from fox and cnn. I don't think there were comments on reddit at then so it got boring quickly.

After the userbase ditched digg for reddit it was fun for a while, you actually got news at least a whole day before it was in the local paper. News on reddit for the past couple of years has been behind even print papers. I would see stuff on the front page days after I saw it on a news outlet, and then reposts for a week.

I don't really think there are many parallels between the reddit fiasco and digg dying, other than the userbase migrating.

For actual news these days, I rely on things like my local news website, google/bing news and slashdot for tech stuff. For user generated content and fun commentary, there is Voat :)

From what I remember:

  • A lot of frustration about power-users (remember MrBabyMan?) controlling what made it to the front page. Remember there were no subs, so if it didn't get there it basically went unseen.
  • There were several leaked discussions of a right-wing agenda controlling what was visible, with digg/bury brigades heavily influencing everything. In its defence, Digg management/staff had no part in this, it was the power-users. That said they could have done more to prevent it.
  • The whole "social" thing. Following users, trying to turn it into Twitter or Facebook. Ruined the experience.
  • Trolls and spam, the same huge ASCII art comments everywhere, and extremely poor quality discussion. It turned into an idiocracy. Picture /r/funny with nowhere else to go.

And of course the v4 redesign. That was the bullet that put the horse down and even the most hardcore Digg defenders threw in the towel and came to reddit with their tails between their legs.

Like deja vu... all over again.
But seriously, it's all I could think of... "here we go again" (in a good way). The internet routs around censorship like it's a disease.

There's differences of course, but the core pattern is the same. The sites both took a very distinct shift towards money and away from what made them what they are. You could smell the VC's and Business Majors taking over. And the userbase revolted.

See, what "they" don't get is that we don't need to put up with their sh*t.
We're here for our reasons, not theirs. The instant it changes, we leave. That's what happened to Digg. It's what's happening to Reddit.

The contrast in sites was more pronounced though.
Digg was a very different site than Reddit. Voat has some interesting differences, but it's pretty damn similar.
So there was a much greater sense of "Digg invading".

The drop in quality was the same though... Digg went down the girgler overnight. Reddit's taking a slower dive in some subreddits, but it's sinking pretty fast none the less.

Once again, I find myself sitting back watching the fireworks.
